lead: Two counting problems share one toolkit. A derangement is a permutation in which nothing lands back in its own place — four letters into four addressed envelopes with every letter wrong. A distribution problem places r balls into n boxes under rules: balls identical or distinct, boxes allowed empty or not. Both show up in testing whether a shuffle fixed anything, in seat-allocation puzzles, in hashing, and in the inclusion–exclusion machinery. Only a few universities teach this as a named topic; the marks come from naming the model correctly before computing.
prereq: You need: 3.2 Permutations and combinations and 3.4 Principle of inclusion and exclusion.

sections.h3: Derangements: nothing in its own place

blocks.text: A derangement is a permutation of n labelled objects in which no object stays in its original position. Write D_n, also written !n, for the count. The small values are D_1 = 0, D_2 = 1, D_3 = 2, D_4 = 9. The standard model is letters and addressed envelopes: letter i must not go into envelope i.

blocks.where: D_n is the number of derangements of n objects, used for n ≥ 3, with starting values D_1 = 0 and D_2 = 1.

blocks.text: Why the recurrence holds: letter 1 must go into one of the n − 1 wrong envelopes. Say it goes into envelope j. If letter j goes to envelope 1, the two letters have swapped and the other n − 2 letters must be deranged: D_{n−2} ways. If letter j avoids envelope 1, then the remaining n − 1 letters carry exactly the original restriction: D_{n−1} ways.

blocks.where: n! counts all permutations; the alternating sum cancels the ones with fixed letters, k counting how many letters are fixed. The ratio D_n/n! tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368.

sections.h3: Stars and bars: identical balls into distinct boxes

blocks.text: Place r identical balls into n distinct boxes, empty boxes allowed. Write r stars in a row; n − 1 bars cut that row into n groups. Each placement is one such string, and each string is one placement.

blocks.where: C(a, b) = a!/(b!(a − b)!) is the binomial coefficient, r is the number of identical balls, n is the number of distinct boxes. With r = 10 and n = 4: C(13, 3) = 286 placements.

blocks.text: If no box may stay empty, give one ball to each box first and distribute the rest: C(r − 1, n − 1) placements, possible only when r ≥ n.
Make the r balls distinct and the n boxes distinct, empties allowed. Each ball chooses a box on its own, so the product rule gives n^r placements.
Forcing every box to be used is an onto-function count. Inclusion–exclusion over the boxes left empty:

blocks.where: k is the number of boxes forced empty, (n − k)^r places the r distinct balls into the remaining boxes, and the sum is 0 when r < n. For n = 3 boxes and r = 4 balls: 81 − 48 + 3 = 36.

figure.caption: Letter A sits in envelope 2, B in 1, C in 4, D in 3, so every letter is in a wrong envelope. This is one of the nine derangements of four letters.

spec.title: One derangement of 4 letters
spec.aria: A letter row A, B, C, D is matched to envelope row 2, 1, 4, 3, so no letter is in its own envelope.

examples.question: Four letters A, B, C, D are placed one each into four addressed envelopes. Find the number of placements in which no letter reaches its own envelope. Solve by inclusion–exclusion, then verify with the recurrence and with the factorial formula.
steps: Total placements of 4 distinct letters into 4 envelopes: 4! = 24.
Let A_i be the set of placements where letter i is correct. Then |A_i| = 3! = 6, and there are C(4, 1) = 4 such sets: 4 × 6 = 24.
Triples: |A_i ∩ A_j ∩ A_k| = 1! = 1, with C(4, 3) = 4 triples: 4 × 1 = 4.
All four correct: 0! = 1, with C(4, 4) = 1 set: 1.
examples.answer: Exactly 9 of the 24 placements leave every letter in a wrong envelope.
examples.check:
from math import factorial, comb
n = 4
ie = sum((-1)**k * comb(n, k) * factorial(n - k) for k in range(n + 1))
D = [0] * (n + 1)
D[1], D[2] = 0, 1
for i in range(3, n + 1):
    D[i] = (i - 1) * (D[i - 1] + D[i - 2])
fac = factorial(n) * sum((-1)**k / factorial(k) for k in range(n + 1))
print(ie)
print(D[n])
print(round(fac))

traps: Writing n! or (n − 1)! as the derangement count. D_4 = 9, not 24 and not 6.
Using n^r when the balls are identical. Identical balls give C(r + n − 1, n − 1), a far smaller number.
Dropping the factor (n − 1) in the recurrence, or starting the recurrence at D_1 = 1 when D_1 = 0.
Confusing the two no-empty-box answers: C(r − 1, n − 1) for identical balls but inclusion–exclusion for distinct balls.
Off-by-one in the binomial: it is C(r + n − 1, n − 1), with n − 1 bars, not n.

quiz.q: Define a derangement of n labelled objects.
quiz.a: A permutation in which no object stays in its original position; the count is written D_n or !n.

quiz.q: State the recurrence for D_n and its two starting values.

quiz.a: One letter in one envelope is always in its own envelope, so nothing can be deranged: D_1 = 0. With two letters the only wrong arrangement is the swap, so D_2 = 1.

quiz.q: Distribute 7 identical sweets into 3 distinct boxes, empty boxes allowed. Count the placements.
quiz.a: Stars and bars: C(7 + 3 − 1, 3 − 1) = C(9, 2) = 36 placements.

quiz.q: Place 4 distinct balls into 2 distinct boxes so that neither box is empty. Count the placements.
quiz.a: Total 2^4 = 16; subtract the 2 placements with one box empty: 16 − 2 = 14.

quiz.q: Compute D_5 from D_3 and D_4 and state the ratio D_5/5!.
Five letters are placed at random into five envelopes. Find the probability that no letter is correct, and say how it compares with n = 4.
quiz.a: D_5 = 44, total 5! = 120, so the probability is 44/120 = 11/30 ≈ 0.367. For n = 4 it was 9/24 = 0.375; the value moves closer to 1/e as n grows.

beyond: Not for the exam. Derangement counts model matching problems where nobody may receive their own item, and the same alternating sum drives the hat-check puzzle and card-shuffle bets. The onto count is n! times the Stirling number of the second kind S(r, n), which counts partitions of r distinct objects into n non-empty blocks. Hashing analysis uses onto counts when every bucket must be touched. Good search words: Stirling numbers of the second kind, hat-check problem, rook polynomial.
